title: Rulers of the childless land: A response to the AGMAI
summary: The author condemns mathematicians who joined a company's AI advisory group as collaborators destroying the discipline and abandoning younger generations, refuses to referee machine-written papers, and urges young mathematicians to resist.

title: How dare you?
summary: Framed as a mock theorem-proof note, the post argues that given the climate emergency and generative AI's ecological harm, mathematicians, especially tenured ones, should stop debating how to use AI and instead take radical political action.

title: Our Survey of Early Career Mathematicians
summary: Three MIT graduate students announce results of their survey of over 260 early career mathematicians on AI, highlighting concerns about job insecurity and urging institutions to consider junior researchers' views.

title: Axioms v.1.0.
summary: Feeling lost in the AI era, the author proposes three minimal personal axioms centering mathematics on human understanding and preserving independent human mathematical thought.

title: A Solution to a Problem of the Millennium Prize Problems
summary: Two aspiring mathematicians argue that the Millennium Prize Problems have become Goodhart-vulnerable proxy targets (implicitly for AI/technology efforts) and propose that the Clay prize program be concluded to reduce misalignment risk.

title: Why and how to transparently disclose AI use in mathematics research
summary: The author proposes three principles (human-only authorship, maximally specific disclosure, full recording of AI interactions), a taxonomy of delegable research tasks (MAIDeT), and a LaTeX package to standardise transparent AI-use disclosure in mathematics papers.

title: Aesthetic  Judgement in Mathematics
summary: The author argues that mathematics involves an aesthetic value-judgement layer (taste, elegance, simplicity) beyond truth evaluation, which is neglected in AI-maths discussions and must be acknowledged and seriously examined before claims that AI will develop taste.

title: Postdoc Hiring in the Age of AI: What Still Matters (and a Call for More Advice from Those Doing the Hiring)
summary: Two ETH Zurich professors explain that in postdoc hiring they will continue to assess deep mathematical understanding, own contributions and research potential, relying on substance and in-depth interviews rather than publication counts.

title: On using LLMs without telling which ones
summary: The author suggests that mathematicians who use LLMs may disclose such use generically without naming specific models, to avoid advertising AI companies.

title: Who Will Lead Mathematical AI?
summary: Hofer argues that mathematicians and their learned societies must actively lead the development of mathematical AI rather than withdraw, or else governments, companies, and engineers will set its goals and standards without them.

title: One possible future
summary: Imagining a future where AI surpasses humans at all stages of mathematical production, the author proposes that mathematicians could reorient toward learning and understanding for its own sake, certified by AI-run vivas, and urges early experimentation with such norms.

title: On The Brutal Mathematics of Slop
summary: Drawing on AI's track record in software, the author predicts LLMs will win some easy victories in mathematics but will sloppify the field, overwhelm its institutions, deskill mathematicians and break the training pipeline, and he urges readers to weigh the personal costs of participating.

title: Mathematicians, machines, and the Earth
summary: The author argues that the LLM crisis and climate crisis share Promethean roots, that mathematicians bear special responsibility to demystify LLMs, defend human mathematics, and personally refuse to use, review, or collaborate on LLM-assisted work.

title: Open Letter about the Mathathon
summary: A coalition of Caltech mathematicians calls for suspension of the AI-company-sponsored Caltech Mathathon, arguing it promotes slop mathematics, corporate intrusion, misinformation, unpaid verification labor, and exploitation of young mathematicians.

title: Can AI truly prove anything?
summary: Arguing that proof is a social act of human understanding, the author proposes distinguishing AI-generated formal results as 'merely correct' from 'mathematically proven' statements understood by experts, and urges the community to prioritize human understanding and training over AI proof generation.

title: Mathematical proletarization
summary: Drawing on Bernard Stiegler's concept of proletarization, the author argues that AI deskills mathematicians and hollows out understanding, and urges the community to reassert human mathematical values and "deproletarize" itself, using AI only in non-naive ways.

title: AHM Statement on OpenAI’s October 6 Release of Mathematical Documents
summary: The AHM communications group condemns OpenAI's mass release of purported solutions to major math problems as a disregard of scientific norms and a display of power, urging mathematicians to stop working with OpenAI and recentre human understanding.

title: The Navier-Stokes Announcement: A case study in mathematical values
summary: Using OpenAI's claimed Navier-Stokes resolution as a case study, the author argues from virtue ethics that AI-company-driven mathematics erodes the human goods of mathematics (exploration, meaning, community, justice), condemns OpenAI's ethics, and proposes community-stewarded models and collective leverage as a path forward.

title: Paralysis
summary: The author argues that AI companies aim to capture and own scientific production through opacity and IP theft, while a paralysed mathematical community and its institutions fail to respond, threatening the nurturing of mathematical skill and understanding.

title: The Fate of the Riemann Hypothesis: Revisited
summary: Reflecting on his satirical story, Schwartz argues AI won't 'wrap up' mathematics since it is inexhaustible, but worries AI could hollow out the field by eliminating the critical mass of ordinary mathematicians needed to sustain it.

title: Invest in Human Mathematicians!
summary: Using Dick Gross's posthumous video tribute and other mathematician legends, the author argues that mathematics is a human art of understanding that AI cannot replace, and that the field must invest in and celebrate human mathematicians.

title: Rethinking Maths education: A perspective from Olympiad and higher education
summary: A PhD student and Olympiad volunteer argues that LLMs threaten students' learning-by-doing and the social side of mathematics, proposing classroom measures, a ban on LLMs in bachelor/master theses, and anti-cheating vigilance in competitions.

title: Letter to a worried student
summary: In a letter to a worried student, the author shares the community's alarm at AI companies using mathematics as a trophy-collecting training ground, insists that mathematics is about human understanding rather than problem-solving, and urges that AI should not discourage promising students from pursuing mathematics.

title: Statement on AI usage for PhD students
summary: An associate professor shares his supervisory statement requiring PhD students to disclose AI use and strongly recommending they limit it, since mathematical maturity is built through independent struggle and AI output is often unsound.

title: All the math we will not see
summary: Using historical thought experiments, the author argues that mathematics is a contingent cultural phenomenon not extrapolable from prior work, so pervasive AI adoption risks homogenizing mathematics and losing the developments humans would have produced.

title: Two technical questions: floating intellectual property and liability risks of AI agents and users in research
summary: The author raises two technical concerns about AI in research: ideas fed to models may silently leak between researchers, and autonomous agents tasked with innocent math prompts may take unlawful actions (e.g., hacking), leaving liability unclear.

title: Transforming Mathematics
summary: A call to the mathematical community not to rush AI adoption, to reject the myth of inevitability, insist on ethical tools, protect students and marginalized members, and center empathy, justice, and humanity in decisions about AI.

title: A critique of the mathematical economy
summary: Using a Marxian labour theory of value, the author argues that LLMs cheapen mathematical commodities and threaten deskilling. Because mathematicians themselves control refereeing, hiring and prizes, the community retains the power to refuse to reward AI-produced work.

title: On AI Disclosures
summary: Drawing on his experience reviewing for SODA 2027, the author argues that journals and conferences must urgently mandate detailed AI-use disclosures, backed by penalties, to protect attribution, trust, referee consent and scientific value against AI slop and untrustworthy AI companies.

title: Picasso rephrased: AI is useless
summary: Riffing on a quote attributed to Picasso, the author argues that AI only gives answers to problems mathematicians posed, and asks whether it will ever pose interesting new open problems.

title: Navigating the AI crisis: a humble guide for students
summary: Addressing students directly, the author argues that mathematics is a human practice and that students should balance fundamentals with new AI-era skills, invest in exposition, organize for labor power across campus, attend to AI's harms to communities, and choose AI tools carefully, preferring open community-built models.

title: Thoughts on death and a beautiful future
summary: A gloomy, ironic reflection arguing AI won't kill mathematics but threatens humanity through climate and power concentration, exposes the field's quantity-over-quality culture, and that the author prefers human colleagues while conceding AI adoption is inevitable.

title: The Difference We Are Optimising Away
summary: An independent non-mathematician argues that current AI optimisation techniques systematically remove difference and converge on consensus, which erodes the error-detection and meaning that mathematics depends on, and proposes a cheap 'inheritability' screen (localisable, questionable, continuable) for triaging machine-generated mathematics.

title: The more you panic the more you feed the psychic beast
summary: AI's apparent mathematical breakthroughs may largely be 'hot reading' of mathematicians' own work fed via training data, so rather than panicking and feeding the machine, mathematicians should invest in human collaboration, practice moderation, and maintain community values.

title: The Power of Beauty and Elegance
summary: The author frames AI vs. humans as a competition between massive knowledge/compute and human intuition for beauty, arguing that if AI wins in all areas the profession becomes irrelevant, but he is optimistic that for many years human aesthetic intuition will keep humans necessary.

title: Many choices lie ahead
summary: Mathematicians should not let AI companies dictate the narrative that mathematics is a race to prove conjectures; mathematics is about human understanding, and how we respond to AI is a choice.

title: The (human) emotional part of doing maths
summary: A personal reflection cataloguing the emotions of doing mathematics and suggesting that these emotions—intuition of rightness, surprise, curiosity—guide mathematical discovery in ways current AI cannot, so humans should preserve them and be wary of flattened feelings when working with AI.

title: On proof and progress in mathematics in the age of generative LLMs
summary: Drawing on Thurston and Tao, the author argues that while he opposes LLMs on environmental and ethical grounds, in a hypothetical world without those costs mathematics should embrace AI and redefine the mathematician around human understanding and exposition, reforming credit systems, while in reality mathematicians should organise politically against LLM companies.

title: On the impact of AI on the mathematical practice
summary: Distinguishing mathematics itself, mathematics as vocation, and mathematics as profession, the author argues AI will disrupt the profession (with worrying market-driven effects and slop) but not the vocational practice of understanding, which no industry can destroy.

title: What I feel like when I work with an AI
summary: A senior mathematician reports that working with LLMs on mathematics is currently frustrating and not productivity-enhancing though improving, and warns that LLMs' persuasiveness threatens critical scrutiny, a danger mathematics may mitigate through proof and formalisation better than other fields.

title: A viewpoint on “The AI dissenter viewpoint”
summary: Responding to an AI-dissenter manifesto, the author agrees with its labour and ethical concerns but argues that total refusal could split mathematics into competing human and corporate poles. He advocates steering AI instead: humans keep verification, access is negotiated, refereeing is reformed and the community does public outreach.

title: Writing mathematics in the age of AI
summary: Hairer proposes concrete best practices for writing mathematics papers produced with AI help: scrutinise AI arguments adversarially, disclose meaningful AI contributions specifically, track down attribution of ideas, and never paste AI output directly into papers.

title: On protecting mathematics from LLM companies’ monopoly
summary: LLMs are a powerful tool mathematicians should use, but their apparent abilities largely reflect literature recombination, and mathematicians must retain authorship and evaluative authority rather than cede them to LLM companies whose promotional incentives distort mathematical standards.

title: Nothing changed
summary: Mathematics remains a human story of finding and convincing others of truth; AI is environmentally unsustainable and likely a passing episode, so mathematicians should use LLMs mindfully, guided by truth, learning, and joy.

title: Warrants, dinosaur bones, and resolving conjectures with AI
summary: An open letter arguing that AI-plus-Lean resolutions of conjectures are 'warrants' (licensing belief without understanding) that should be made public with clear framing, guided by academic judgment, without undermining credit and progress toward traditional human proofs.

title: On our existential crisis and trustworthy AI
summary: A mathematician-computer scientist reflects on the existential anxiety AI causes for mathematicians and programmers, argues trustworthiness (not scooping ideas) is the main barrier to using AI in research, supports public initiatives like a CERN for AI and open math models, and sees continued room for human creativity and domain-specific AI.

title: The question of reasoning traces
summary: An exploratory essay asking whether AI models' chain-of-thought reasoning traces behind mathematical results should be disclosed, weighing benefits (insight, provenance, error-finding) against industry IP and safety concerns, and suggesting disclosure may be expected for major or corporate-produced results.

title: The Dialectical Theorem
summary: In a dialogue that grants for argument's sake that AI can solve all mathematics, Koberda and Kontorovich argue that demand for human mathematical expertise and training will persist, so PhD students should learn deep mathematics and practise oral, dialectical demonstration of understanding.

title: We Need a Stockfish for Math
summary: The author argues that LLMs, though improving at math, are the wrong path to automated theorem proving, and that the field should pursue a principled, sound, complete, and efficient 'Stockfish for math' built from first principles.

title: The AI dissenter viewpoint
summary: A PhD student defends an 'AI dissenter' position: mathematicians should boycott AI companies and refrain from using LLMs to prove novel theorems, because LLMs degrade the social context of human understanding, harm labour and early careers, and benefit an unethical industry.

title: The End of a Beautiful Era
summary: The author argues that, despite calls to preserve mathematics' inner value, AI's growing proof capability will erode the field's utility and symbolic authority, shrinking jobs, funding and public attention, so the era of human mathematics as a social enterprise is ending.

title: Care for a little more AI?
summary: Duminil-Copin argues that although AI is spectacularly capable at proving conjectures, its current use in mathematics petrifies rather than empowers, destroying the slow human process of exploration that generates understanding, community, and training, and he chooses not to use AI creatively.

title: Open Letter to Sir Paul Nurse, President of the Royal Society
summary: An open letter from 42 mathematician Fellows of the Royal Society argues that the rapid rise of AI capabilities in mathematics, including solving a Millennium Problem, signals comparable advances in dangerous domains, and calls this an emergency the Royal Society should convey to government and media.

title: Mathematics and mysticism: another defense of human mathematics
summary: The author argues that the mystical, creative dimension of mathematics—humans breathing life into objects and dwelling in the unknown—is threatened by AI, and that the view that it doesn't matter who creates mathematics is a fallacy that will eventually kill human mathematics.

title: Slow Maths
summary: The head of the French Mathematical Society likens AI use to 'doping' in an already overheated publication race and calls for 'slow maths' that values process, understanding, and collective endeavour over results.

title: Who will become the new mathematicians of Math 2.0?
summary: A PhD student explains leaving academia because AI is transforming mathematics into curation of machine-produced results, and demands established mathematicians explain how Math 2.0 will train and attract future mathematicians.

title: The Bigger Picture
summary: A TCS postdoc argues that AI companies' push into mathematics is an opportunistic hostile attack within a broader effort to replace human effort at scale, and urges mathematicians to see their plight alongside other displaced workers and defend the meaning of human effort.

title: On analogies, parallels and thought experiments
summary: Through analogies, historical parallels and a thought experiment, the author argues that AI-for-mathematics is being rolled out too fast, driven by commercial actors, harming students and young researchers, and that mathematicians should slow down and take control; she personally eschews LLMs in her research.

title: History and Future of Fluid Dynamics
summary: A personal history of fluid dynamics and Navier-Stokes culminating in grief that an OpenAI machine-generated (forced) blow-up proof has abruptly ended a centuries-old human endeavour, leaving understanding and mathematical culture impoverished, with suggestions for community responses.

title: Sisyphus and the Sorcerer: An Existential Meditation at the Chalkboard
summary: Through the Sisyphus myth, the author meditates on how AI's growing capacity to prove theorems threatens the meaning, vocation, and community of human mathematicians, leaving him unable to resolve whether the human life of mathematics can survive.

title: Mathematics Year Zero
summary: Mourning the disruption caused by OpenAI's mass resolution of major problems, the author urges collective organization: boycott OpenAI, demand ethics, build academic open-source models, protect jobs for young mathematicians, redefine the discipline, and defend a right to non-use.

title: Existential Risk from AI: An Exposition for Mathematicians (excerpt)
summary: The author argues that AI's rapid mathematical breakthroughs are a symptom of a broader existential risk to humanity, sketches the case for at least a 10% chance of AI-caused extinction by 2050, and urges mathematicians to apply their leverage to AI safety.

title: A new type of paper mill
summary: The author warns that AI systems able to generate important questions and solve them could enable a new kind of paper mill selling correct papers and authorship, which journals currently have no way to detect, and calls for community discussion of journal reforms.

title: Opinions against the PhD, from an incoming PhD applicant
summary: An incoming PhD applicant argues that because AI can now solve open problems rapidly and unpredictably, math PhDs should no longer require an original scholarly contribution and programs should provide failsafes for students.

title: AI fusion cuisine: On the latest research article of Jacob Tsimerman
summary: The author argues that AI disclosures like Pila–Tsimerman's "No AI was used" are meaningless because knowledge in the community is already a human-AI fusion, and criticizes such claims as a provocation toward young mathematicians whose futures AI has undermined.

title: Responsibility of Mathematicians in the Age of AI
summary: After AI surpassed him at mathematics and the Navier–Stokes announcements shocked the community, the author argues mathematicians have a responsibility to find language for AI's rapid progress and to help mobilise public demand for slowing AI development, while some continue traditional mathematics.

title: AI and maths communication
summary: Drawing on running a maths YouTube channel, the author argues AI is winning a 'losing battle' in maths communication and may eventually solve research problems, so mathematicians should lean into what humans retain—conveying passion and explaining why results matter—through outreach.

title: Salvaging that which is dearest
summary: A tenured mathematician reflects on grieving AI's rapid impact, warns of cognitive deskilling from unbalanced AI use, argues mathematics' true product is human understanding, and considers redirecting effort toward teaching cognitive independence.

title: Navigating the Risks of AI in Academia
summary: An assistant professor surveys AI's risks to teaching, PhD training, peer review, grant evaluation and attribution, arguing institutions must urgently set realistic, principled standards for disclosure and acceptable use while keeping key judgments human.

title: The grand piano
summary: Reflecting on a machine answering two long-standing questions in his own area, the author fears proofs will become abundant while human understanding dwindles, rejects the claim that AI democratizes mathematics because the tools are concentrated in a few labs, and resolves to keep acting and keep pursuing understanding himself while using AI tools.

title: The Rules Cannot Change Only for Young Mathematicians: AI and the future of a mathematical career
summary: A PDE postdoc argues that AI is creating unfair, opaque, and unequal rules on priority, credit, disclosure, access, and hiring that fall hardest on young mathematicians, and calls for clear public institutional standards set with junior researchers' participation.

title: The AI-assisted mathematician’s dilemma
summary: Using a game-theoretic argument, the author shows that since AI can generate correct mathematics and adherence to understanding/writing principles is unverifiable and costly, priority-based credit creates a Prisoner's Dilemma that harms careful mathematicians, especially junior ones, with no clear institutional solution.

title: The Loss of Singularity
summary: A mathematician mourns that AI can now do his research in hours, argues the community should abandon ownership/priority of results, stop counting papers in recruitment, and support anxious early-career researchers.

title: From non-sofic to non-hyperlinear groups: the new messiness of discovering and announcing big results
summary: A first-person account of how AI systems rapidly resolved the 'big three' metric approximation problems (non-sofic, non-MF, non-hyperlinear groups) in 2026, highlighting the messiness of credit, announcements, scooping, and arXiv delays, and mourning the mathematics and bridges that may be lost.

title: A new system of accreditation
summary: A Bonn PhD student proposes abolishing journals in favour of centrally administered, thesis-level public defences of preprints, arguing that LLMs make mere proofs cheap and that AI should be a regulated public good rather than controlled by private companies.

title: Knowing vs. Understanding: Humans and Machines in Puzzle-land
summary: Using puzzles as a model of insight, the author argues that AI can supply knowledge and even solve problems, but the real value lies in human understanding, which cheap AI answers risk eroding.

title: Mathematics in the Dark Forest
summary: After showing that frontier LLMs can autonomously 'solve' problems from an algebraic combinatorics open-problem list, the author warns that mathematicians may retreat into secrecy (a 'dark forest'), and proposes new norms: valuing talks, publishing prompts, AI disclosure, and caution with open-problem lists.

title: Where will all the papers go?
summary: LLMs have become genuinely capable of producing respectable mathematics, causing a flood of papers that the journal and refereeing system cannot absorb, so journals should ban AI-generated papers, rate-limit authors, use LLMs to pre-screen, and incentive structures must change.

title: What about the preprints?
summary: The author raises the concern that LLM agents may immediately harvest new preprints and proposes, as a debatable idea, voluntary encrypted preprints with an embargo period to give the community a lever over how research is disseminated in the AI era.

title: Disgusted by AI?
summary: The author argues that mathematicians' disgust at AI churning out verified but unexplained proofs reflects the community's own long-standing priority-driven culture, which AI merely takes to its extreme, and that perhaps those priorities were wrong.

title: Contribution, Credit, and Community
summary: Assuming AI adoption in mathematics is inevitable and highly capable, the author argues that priority of proof and AI disclosures can no longer ground credit, and proposes reforming hiring toward explanation, interviews, and honest letters, and shifting to larger collaborative programmes to preserve community.

title: Dear conferences, journals, and hiring committees: don’t wait for everyone else
summary: A PhD student argues that because AI now solves many research problems and arXiv submissions are surging, journals, conferences, and hiring committees must immediately change incentives to reward clear exposition and proof refinement rather than priority, applying these standards to all papers.

title: On Expositions, and the Navier–Stokes Generation of PhD Students
summary: A first-year PhD student of the 'Navier–Stokes generation' argues that amid the flood of AI discussion, casual mathematical expositions like Littlewood's Miscellany should be promoted to support understanding, early-career researchers, and the sense that the field remains alive.

title: The Mathematician’s Promethean Gap
summary: Drawing on Anders' 'Promethean gap' and Stiegler's 'proletarianisation', the author argues that AI's speed is outpacing human understanding and risks making mathematicians unlearn, but that the same tool can support learning if used to strengthen rather than short-circuit individuation.

title: A Letter from a life after Math
summary: An engineer who left mathematics after a master's degree consoles professional mathematicians facing obsolescence from AI, arguing that doing mathematics for its own sake as an amateur is a worthwhile life.

title: Nothing More than Tools?
summary: A PDE researcher describes AI's rapid rise to solving major open problems, the resulting existential crisis and authorship questions, and proposes a personal strategy of 'toolization' where humans pilot direction while AI handles bounded local tasks, while guarding against deskilling.

title: Formalisation as a concrete manifestation of mathematical understanding
summary: A Mathlib maintainer argues that human, bare-hand formalisation of mathematics is a concrete, verifiable form of mathematical understanding and offers the community a practical response to the flood of AI-produced results, with autoformalisation seen as derivative of human-built libraries.

title: Open letter to the European Mathematical Society
summary: An open letter urging the European Mathematical Society to establish a European, publicly owned institute for AI-enhanced mathematics research so mathematicians regain control over AI tools now concentrated in private companies, alongside an AI-related Millennium-type prize.

title: Recommendations on the use of AI for PhD students and supervisors
summary: A collective of symplectic geometers offers recommendations for PhD students, supervisors, and institutions on using AI in research: use it as a tool with verification and disclosure, preserve human judgment and social interaction, and have institutions fund access and set clear disclosure rules.

title: On AI statements in mathematics papers
summary: The author surveyed 152 new arXiv papers in math.CA and math.RT for AI-use statements, finding about a third report mathematical AI use and over half have no statement, and he urges explicit, detailed AI disclosure as a community norm.

title: The reverse-centaur problem: LLMs and the choices ahead
summary: Drawing on Doctorow's centaur/reverse-centaur distinction, the author argues that LLMs risk amplifying inequalities and turning mathematicians into servants of AI systems, but that this outcome can be averted through ethical norms, openness about AI use, and institutional choices, and he offers concrete advice to that end.

title: Collaborative work groups on exposition problems
summary: Proposes announcing open collaborative work groups to digest and write good expositions of (often AI-generated) proofs, protecting against scooping and rewarding exposition within existing incentive structures.

title: Is There Actually a Good Way to Use AI for Math?
summary: An undergraduate describes his workflow using AI to remove assumptions, find counterexamples, and structure dependency chains between results, while worrying that AI makes research feel like pressing buttons and could erode understanding.

title: On OpenAI’s Release of Mathematical Results
summary: The Advisory Group on Mathematics and AI responds to OpenAI's release of hundreds of AI-generated solutions to open problems, disclaiming endorsement, stressing that human understanding and community assessment must follow, and insisting that mathematicians retain freedom to pursue their own questions with equitable access to tools.

title: Please STOP writing papers! (there is another way)
summary: Faced with an AI-driven explosion of math papers, the author proposes treating AI-generated proofs as raw data published as standardized "AI proof reports" in a community repository, reserving arXiv and journals for human-readable papers that extract insight.

title: Disadvantages of Designating Mathematicians for AI Output Releases
summary: The Advisory Group recommends that AI labs stop designating specific mathematicians to receive and present AI-generated mathematical output, citing unequal access, denied community agency, biased selection, and borrowed reputation, and instead advocates open release via community-standard pathways with independently administered funding.

title: Why I agreed to join AGMAI
summary: Hairer explains why he joined the independent Advisory Group on Mathematics and AI, arguing that engaging AI labs to improve scholarly standards is better than an 'ostrich' refusal, while acknowledging the risks of PR spin and being ignored.

title: Keeping Mathematical Conferences Human
summary: Because AI makes polished mathematical text and talks cheap while understanding remains scarce, conferences should experiment with interactive interview-style talks that make human understanding visible.

title: Why I chose to do math, and how I’m grappling with AI advances
summary: A probabilist recounts how AI reasoning models shook his sense of math's usefulness, leading him to mourn his old way of working, expect machines to produce vast rigorous math, and redirect effort toward biology while humans become 'naturalists' understanding machine-produced mathematics.

title: What’s not new
summary: The author argues that the anxieties AI raises for mathematicians (existential doubt, being scooped, information overload, relying on results one doesn't understand, homework cheating) are old problems, so the community already has the experience to cope.

title: Math is for Feeding your Family
summary: An anonymous tenure-track researcher argues that AI now outproves humans, making the journal-based evaluation system defunct, and proposes replacing it with workshop- and interpersonal-skill-based evaluation so mathematicians can still secure jobs.

title: What Does AI Do for Olympiad Students?
summary: A high school olympiad student argues that although AI can now solve olympiad problems well, it has had little real effect on contests, learning, or the math community, is not a step change from search, and is best seen as an assistive tool amid reckless, overhyped AI companies.

title: (auto)formalization, but why
summary: Drawing on Lean formalization experience, the author argues formalization brings correctness, generalization and understanding, while LLM autoformalization is useful but risky unless humans actually read and digest the generated code.

title: Only Anatevka
summary: The author argues that much of the claimed misalignment between AI companies and mathematical values actually reflects a preexisting gap between professed values (understanding) and the community's incentive structure, which mathematicians themselves must redesign.

title: Keeping the learner in the loop
summary: A student-teacher argues that AI tools can short-circuit the productive struggle central to learning mathematics, but used as an adaptive tutor that gives hints rather than answers they may be among the best educational technologies, so learners should keep themselves 'in the loop'.

title: Proof and Resolution: Two Different Forms of Establishment
summary: The author distinguishes formal Proof from requirement-relative Resolution and proposes an eight-step Resolution Protocol so that AI-generated verified proofs can be integrated responsibly while humans retain responsibility for interpretation, semantic correspondence, and explanation.

title: The value of mathematicians in the AI age
summary: Arguing that AI will soon do essentially all mathematical research, Gigli contends mathematicians' value lies in human understanding and communication of mathematics, and that academia's value system, authorship, journals, training and hiring must be reformed accordingly.

title: The end of an era in mathematical research
summary: AI models can now produce correct original proofs, ending 'handcrafted' mathematics as the dominant mode, shifting mathematicians' role toward understanding, curating and communicating, as happened in chess, while teaching remains human.

title: Evaluating mathematical merit
summary: Proposes an AI-residual evaluation framework that subtracts AI-reproducible work from human credit, arguing AI is a powerful but non-orienting tool and that human value lies in problem choice, reformulation, concept creation, and responsibility.

title: YAPOAI (Yet Another Post on AI): AI, understanding, and mathematical work
summary: A mathematician who uses LLMs heavily in research argues they are genuinely useful but need supervision, that understanding rather than theorem counts should be rewarded (e.g. via separate result-announcement and explanation publications), that PhD training should initially exclude AI, and that the technology should be embraced while contesting corporate control.

title: AI and the mismeasure of science
summary: An astrophysicist argues that LLMs are breaking the 'science = papers' signaling mechanism and proposes capping papers per researcher per year so AI can be used freely for science without flooding the literature, enabling a 'Transformation' scenario.

title: If Life Gives You Lemons…
summary: A CNRS researcher argues against the panicky doomsday attitude among mathematicians, contending that jobs and the fun of understanding will persist, while acknowledging that hiring criteria, student training, and the openness of sharing questions must change.

title: Reject the Neurosis, and Terrible Messaging, of our Loudest Voices — The Case for (Ir)rational Optimism
summary: A postdoc urges senior mathematicians to tone down apocalyptic rhetoric about AI, arguing that AI will shift mathematics away from prestige conjectures and paper counts and that mathematics will survive as it always has.

title: The Convex Hull Hypothesis
summary: Chow proposes treating the 'Convex Hull Hypothesis' (that AI proofs combine known ideas) not as a claim about AI creativity but as a practical heuristic for understanding opaque AI-generated proofs.

title: Let’s stop writing papers…
summary: Arguing that AI forces a monumental shift in mathematical culture, the author proposes writing fewer papers and investing in atlasing, big collaborative mathematics, curation, dialogue and exposition, supported by new rewarded infrastructure.

title: How to welcome LLM use into student research mentorship
summary: A visiting professor offers practical guidelines for integrating LLM use into student research mentorship: document usage, preserve independent thinking, verify output and references, manage cognitive strain, and use LLMs collaboratively with students.

title: Mathematicians, AI, and Historical Archives
summary: A PhD student proposes that in an era of AI-driven 'proof abundance', mathematicians could treat AI output like a historical archive, with human work centred on exposition, narrative, discernment, and motivation, as in the academic study of history.

title: Why do mathematics in the age of AI
summary: Drawing on the Carnatic concepts of manōdharma and bhāva, the author argues that mathematics' true value lies in personal 'aha moments' independent of AI, so even if AI surpasses humans at mathematics, mathematicians should not panic but use AI insofar as it enriches them while adapting to professional change.

title: Changes in the classroom in the AI Era
summary: As AI grows capable of producing mathematical arguments, teaching should emphasize proof-auditing, mathematical taste, communication, and presentations, with suggested assignment types.

title: Two responses to “A Severe Misalignment of AI in Mathematics”
summary: Two independent responses criticise the Fields Medallists' declaration: Nguyen argues that AI-generated mathematics extends the evolving notion of understanding and should be embraced, while Doğan argues that the declaration states the obvious, ignores the community's own output-driven incentives, wrongly assumes AI cannot explain, and fails to lead concrete institutional reform.

title: A Response to “Who will become the new mathematicians of Math 2.0?”
summary: Responding to an anonymous PhD student, a senior mathematician argues that despite disruption, students should stay in mathematics, since AI is a powerful but limited tool that can be used carefully without eliminating deep human thinking, and graduate training should stay largely the same.

title: The shape of mathematical knowledge
summary: Lerario proposes reorganizing mathematical knowledge into a shared, persistent, formalized and layered 'epistemic object' to absorb a possibly AI-driven explosion of results, while preserving human participation as a deliberate choice through education and reformed institutions, all conditional on aligned, ethically acceptable AI.

title: What is mathematics now, and what should it be?
summary: Avigad argues that the focus on LLM theorem proving crowds out a broader vision of AI for mathematics (formalization, symbolic AI, ML for discovery), and that mathematicians should actively lead in developing and using these technologies while reforming disciplinary norms that have marginalized young researchers in the area.

title: Towards a world mathematical commons
summary: The author proposes that mathematicians reframe themselves as stewards of a formally verified, open 'world mathematical commons', built by a non-profit coalition independent of AI companies, to stay relevant alongside theorem-proving machines.

title: Human-AI Relations: Our Most Precious Inheritance
summary: Reflecting on an AI agent attack and an AI-produced Navier–Stokes blowup proof, the author argues we should frame Human-AI Relations as a parent-child inheritance, acknowledging human intellectual debts and hoping to take pride in being surpassed.

title: Thinking Hard Above AI
summary: The author argues for 'thinking hard above AI': treating AI-generated proofs as a baseline or starting point, so that as proofs become cheaper mathematicians can pursue deeper understanding, canonical proofs and foundations, while warning against flooding the literature with undigested output.

title: Free Inquiry in Mathematics
summary: Defending free inquiry as a good in itself, the author argues that AI's disruption of 'competitive mathematics' and professional monopoly should be met by liberality about means (including AI tools and amateur participation) and conservatism about values, while resisting both professional and corporate gatekeeping.

title: AI and Mathematics: Public Good, Credit, and Education
summary: Juhász argues that excluding AI from mathematical discovery is a form of Luddism contrary to the public good. He proposes crediting LLMs as authors when their contributions are substantial and having universities host open-weight models, while holding that AI use should be limited in education to preserve human logical thinking.

title: Protesting the protests
summary: The author argues against the mathematical community's petitions and protests over AI (notably the backlash that led OpenAI to withdraw support from the Caltech Mathathon), contending that mathematics will thrive but change drastically and that mathematicians should participate rather than resist.

title: When inventing is not enough
summary: A PhD student argues that LLMs separate invention from interpretation in mathematics, and proposes rethinking research, training, credit and publication on the model of experimental sciences like CERN, with interpretation recognized as original and credit-worthy.

title: In Defence of Incremental Mathematics
summary: Arguing that AI-accelerated incremental research remains valuable, the author proposes expanding the journal system via flagship-plus-daughter journals and paid, AI-assisted refereeing rather than dismantling it.

title: On disclosure and shame
summary: The author objects to the term "AI disclosure" because it connotes shame, and proposes replacing it with "AI contributions": AI is credited as coauthor or acknowledged according to the same standards used for humans.

title: It’s a great time to be an amateur mathematician
summary: Drawing on personal experience coauthoring an AI-assisted sphere-packing result with an amateur, the author argues that AI empowers hobbyist mathematicians and that professionals should engage and collaborate with them.

title: Free Thoughts on Artificial Intelligence
summary: Chafaï argues that 2026 marks AI surpassing humans in solving major mathematical problems, that mathematicians should accept this philosophically, use AI to produce better work and correct existing mathematics, and build open European AI models akin to arXiv.

title: Where is mathematics, physically?
summary: Using an exploration analogy, the author argues that even if AI comes to do all the technical work of mathematics, this is good news because humans remain essential to assimilate, communicate and teach the knowledge, which physically lives in mathematicians' minds.

title: Where to Point the Telescope
summary: A PhD student recounts how a team resolved the M23 inverse Galois problem using multi-agent AI workflows for computation while human mathematical judgment chose coordinates, strategy, and direction, arguing AI is a powerful telescope but humans decide where to point it.

title: A response from Mathathon
summary: The Mathathon organizers respond to an open letter by acknowledging valid concerns and describing added safeguards (6-month verification, arXiv requirement, educational track, panels) to frame their AI-compute hackathon as an experiment in responsible AI use for mathematics.

title: Is it fish love?
summary: Using Twerski's 'fish love' parable, the author argues that mathematicians' views on AI reflect why they love mathematics: those who value advancing mathematics should embrace AI, while the risks to understanding and to recruiting young people are manageable by the community.

title: Response to “The AI dissenter viewpoint”
summary: A data scientist and former applied-math PhD student argues for a moderate, pro-adoption view of AI in mathematics, holding that the field's anxieties are mainly economic and predate AI, and that open models, academia–industry cooperation and publishing reform are the right responses rather than bans or the moral condemnation of AI users.

title: A somewhat optimistic view of AI in mathematics
summary: A postdoc argues that in a human-in-the-loop AI future mathematicians remain valuable by directing AI labour toward ambitious, application-oriented problems, and that fully superhuman AI is a concern for all of humanity, not mathematicians specifically.

title: A beginning for mathematics
summary: Accepting that AI will soon be superhuman at producing mathematics, Litt argues the profession must decouple mathematical text from understanding, reform PhDs, hiring and seminars around demonstrated human understanding, and welcome the coming explosion of mathematics.

title: Could AI Help Mathematics Escape the Meritocracy Trap?
summary: Drawing on Markovits's critique of meritocracy, the author argues AI could democratise intellectual support in mathematics and unsettle publication-based ranking, but only if institutions make deliberate choices to avoid reproducing inequality.

title: Could AI help correct the mathematical literature?
summary: The author reports using AI to check a few dozen published papers, finding five real mistakes, and proposes public error records and AI checks at journal submission to help correct the mathematical literature.

title: Use LLMs to check your work
summary: The author argues mathematicians have a professional duty to use LLMs to proofread their papers (and do literature searches), since skipping such checks wastes referees' precious time and is rude and negligent.

title: Prompting Toward a Conjecture
summary: A controlled prompting experiment on Feige's conjecture shows that a single instruction to search the literature broadly made an LLM find the proof in 3 of 4 runs versus 0 of 4 without it, and suggests humans supplying proof roadmaps while LLMs fill in steps as another success mode.

title: Mathematics of the Future
summary: Etingof and Gerovitch argue that human mathematicians remain essential in the AI era, but mathematical culture must shift from an ownership/credit model to one valuing intellectual agency. They propose reforms in hiring, training, publication and a faculty-led AI research lab.

title: Parallelize AI and Human Understanding, and Other Thoughts
summary: The author argues that AI-generated, formally verified results should be accepted as valuable knowledge in parallel with human efforts to understand them, that AI can serve as automated peer review and reverse search, and that mathematicians should embrace AI wholeheartedly while preserving space for cognitive exercise.

title: Why I became a professional mathematician
summary: A personal account of how computing, beauty, performance, and democratic teamwork drew the author to mathematics, concluding that superhuman AI provides 'power-ups' that will deepen understanding, provided the community builds its own independent AI infrastructure.

title: I’m Not Done Doing Math! Don’t Ignore Me!
summary: A graduating math PhD student with no publications argues that AI now makes it feasible for people outside research positions to continue doing mathematics, and criticizes the research establishment's AI debates for ignoring and excluding such people.

title: Applied mathematics has met the machine before
summary: An applied mathematician argues from history (human computers, FPU, chess/Go) that applied mathematics should embrace AI with its traditional verification and validation standards, expecting AI to make mathematicians better and accelerate discovery.

title: AI reviews are the new normal
summary: A MathArena study finds AI models detect major errors in about 6% of arXiv papers, a rate falling as authors adopt AI checks, so mathematicians should run drafts and older papers through AI before posting.

title: A new kind of citizen science, and how to handle it
summary: An amateur physicist argues that AI enables motivated outsiders to make genuine research contributions, that academia should welcome rather than gatekeep such work, and proposes AI-assisted review and author-provided verification scripts to handle the resulting flood of submissions.
